content.title: About
content.content: Yuca fries are crispy sticks made from the root of the cassava plant (Manihot esculenta). Cassava, also known as yuca or tapioca, originates from tropical regions of South America and Africa. The fries have a neutral flavor with a faint nutty note and a satisfying crunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cassava is a staple carbohydrate source in many tropical countries, often used as a potato substitute.
The root contains crystalline cellulose, making it resistant to spoilage; it is frequently dried for long‑term storage.
Unlike potatoes, yuca is naturally gluten‑free, suitable for gluten‑free diets.
Traditional dishes like "papa frita" in Peru and Ecuador feature fried yuca served with a spicy ají sauce.
Cassava has a higher starch content than potatoes, giving the fries a denser texture.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Yuca provides starch that digests slowly, helping maintain satiety over time.

items.title: Low in fat when prepared properly
items.content: When baked or air‑fried, yuca fries contain minimal fat, offering a lighter alternative to deep‑fried snacks.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The root contains thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2) and niacin (B3), which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Yuca supplies potassium, magnesium and iron, beneficial for heart and nerve function.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Naturally free of gluten, yuca fries are safe for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Toxicity of raw yuca
items.content: Raw cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides that can be poisonous; thorough cooking eliminates this risk.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because of its high starch content, yuca can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may be allergic to cassava.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions may cause bloating or stomach upset in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve yuca fries hot as a snack, side dish, or in burgers. Sprinkle with salt, paprika, garlic powder, or your favorite seasoning blend. For a healthier option, bake them in the oven with a drizzle of olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry, unprocessed yuca pieces in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked fries should be refrigerated and consumed within 2–3 days, or frozen for up to one month.
